questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question assesses the ability to design a completely branchless, fixed-sequence bit selection algorithm across a 128-bit value—a common requirement for high-performance systems where branches are expensive.

## Key Concepts

- **Branchless bit selection** — no `if`/`switch` in the critical path
- **SWAR-style masks** and prefix sums on 128-bit data
- **128-bit arithmetic** via hi/lo representation
- Handling the edge case when fewer set bits exist than requested

## Approach

Use a divide-and-conquer strategy: first identify which 64-bit block contains the k-th set bit by counting set bits in each half. Then recursively narrow down to smaller block sizes (32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 bits) until the exact position is found. Each step uses only bitwise operations and arithmetic shifts—no branches. If the total population count is ≤ k, return −1 to signal an invalid request.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Constant-time 128-bit comparison is core in cryptography and DB internals to avoid timing channels; probe understanding of lexicographic, boundary handling without branches.

## Key Concepts
- Branchless logic with masks
- Lexicographic 128-bit comparison
- Handling hi/lo boundaries in constant time

## Code Example
```javascript
typedef struct { uint64_t hi; uint64_t lo; } uint128;
static inline int8_t cmp128(uint128 a, uint128 b) {
  int hi = (a.hi > b.hi) - (a.hi < b.hi); // -1,0,1
  int lo = (a.lo > b.lo) - (a.lo < b.lo);
  int m = -(int)(hi != 0); // -1 when hi != 0, else 0
  return (int8_t)((hi & m) | (lo & ~m));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt this to return a sign-agnostic 0/1/2 encoding for a hash comparison?
- Could you prove this runs in constant time regardless of inputs and compiler optimizations?

## Why This Is Asked
Endianness is a practical concern in systems and networking. This question tests precise bit-twiddling with masks and shifts, without relying on loops. It also checks understanding of how a 32-bit word maps to byte positions.

## Key Concepts
- Byte extraction with masks
- Shifting to relocate bytes
- Endianness awareness and portability
- No loops; pure bitwise operations

## Code Example
```c
uint32_t swapEndian32(uint32_t n) {
  return (n >> 24) | ((n >> 8) & 0x0000FF00) | ((n << 8) & 0x00FF0000) | (n << 24);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you generalize to 64-bit values?
- How would you implement an endianness swap for 16-bit values or for an array of 32-bit words efficiently?

Tests the ability to pack multiple fields into a single word, a common task in serialization and network protocols. It emphasizes precise bit-width handling and avoiding branches.

## Key Concepts

- Bitwise masking
- Bit shifts
- Field packing into a 32-bit word

## Code Example

```javascript
function packHeader(version, flags, length) {

}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you validate inputs to prevent overflow or sign issues in languages with signed integers?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of 128-bit shifts, wrap-around logic, and edge cases where n==0. Requires a clean, branch-minimal implementation without loops.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise rotation across 128 bits
- Handling edge cases safely (n==0, 128-n)
- Avoiding undefined shifts across boundary bits

## Code Example
```c
uint128 rotateLeft128(uint128 x, uint8 n) {
  n &= 127;
  if (n == 0) return x;
  return (x << n) | (x >> (128 - n));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt for a language without 128-bit integers?
- How would compiler optimizations affect this implementation in real code?

Tests ability to derive a compact bit check using a single mask instead of branching.

```c
int haveNoConsecutiveOnes32(uint32_t x) {

}
```
